items.question: What is Ajrakh printing?
items.answer: Ajrakh is a natural-dye resist block-printing craft from Kutch in Gujarat, also practised in Barmer and Sindh. The cloth passes through 14 to 20 or more stages of resist paste, mordant printing, indigo and madder dyeing and washing, and a traditional piece is printed on both sides in register.
items.title: Ajrakh Print: How It's Made & How to Wear It – Rutambhara

items.question: Is Ajrakh printed by hand?
items.answer: Genuine Ajrakh is printed with hand-carved wooden blocks, one block per colour per stage. Screen-printed and digital imitations exist; the quickest test is the reverse of the cloth, which on real Ajrakh carries the pattern at nearly full strength.

items.question: Does Ajrakh fabric bleed colour?

items.question: What is the difference between Ajrakh and Bagru or Dabu printing?
items.answer: All three are hand-block resist crafts, but Bagru and Dabu are from Rajasthan and use a mud-and-gum resist with a simpler sequence. Ajrakh is distinguished by its long mordant-and-resist cycle, its indigo and madder palette, and double-sided printing.

items.question: Is Ajrakh silk linen suitable for summer?

items.question: Why is real Ajrakh expensive?
items.answer: Because it takes two to three weeks per length of cloth, uses natural dyes that must be grown and processed, and for double-sided pieces is printed twice, with every block realigned by hand on the reverse.
